title: MB9-19525
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Haiti. She has four children, three of whom reside in Haiti with their aunt; the youngest child was born in Canada in December 2017.

The Appellant alleges she may not return to Haiti because her brother, XXXX (also referred to as XXXX), has harassed, threatened and been violent towards her in the past due to a dispute over family property. The Appellant fears that if she returns to Haiti, her brother will kill her.

According to the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC), she left Haiti in XXXX of 2013 to go first to the Dominican Republic and then on to Brazil. She spent three years in Brazil. She then moved to Mexico with a common-law partner in XXXX 2016, where she stayed several months. In XXXX 2017, at eight months pregnant, the Appellant entered the United States, while her common-law partner remained in Mexico. She entered Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and made a claim for refugee protection.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) determined that the Appellant's allegations lacked credibility and rejected her claim.
The Appellant asserts that the RPD erred in its assessment of her credibility.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 DECISION

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD's finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection was correct. The determinative issue is the lack of credibility of the allegations.

I have attentively listened to the recording of the RPD hearing and I have carefully reviewed the entire record. I have also taken into account the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's allegations are not credible and that the claim should be rejected. The Appellant's failure to mention that her brother wanted to kill her prior to 2008 in her BOC narrative

In her narrative, the Appellant wrote that her father died in 1991, leaving to his successors, several pieces of land and some livestock. She recounted that in 2006, when she would have been roughly 25 years old, she took a piece of land from her brother which he did not want to part with but was due to her as part of her inheritance. The Appellant recounts that in 2008, she built a house on the piece of land but this displeased her brother and from that point on ("dÞs ce temps"), he started to harass and threaten her.2 However, at the hearing, when the Appellant was asked whether she had had any problems with her brother prior to 2008, she replied that yes, that everywhere she went he wanted to kill her and did not want her to live in Haiti.3 The RPD repeated and rephrased the question to ensure that the Appellant understood, however, the Appellant repeated the same answer. When the RPD asked her to explain the discrepancy between her testimony and her BOC narrative, the Appellant was unable to provide a reply which answered the question. Instead she simply stated that she wrote it that way in her story, that is the problem she is facing and that is why she left.4

The Appellant disputes the RPD's finding that this was an 'important omission' from her BOC narrative. The Appellant asserts there was no actual omission because "the appellant did not add any new information in her oral testimony."5 In her memorandum, the Appellant also asserts that she has a limited ability to reply to questions in a straightforward manner. It is submitted: "The appellant, at the very outset of the hearing was asked if she objected to the presence of an observer, an interpreter in training, and with a smiling face nodded her head, and said "Yes." She was asked several times if she objected and several times answered "Yes," before she clarified that it was fine for the interpreter in training to observe her hearing. The fact that the appellant answered "Yes" to whether there was any other disputes before this incident, and then reiterated that the dispute with her brother was regarding the land and as set out in her narrative is not an actual omission, much less an important omission that should have led the Member to make a negative inference as to the appellant's credibility."6

I understand the Appellant's point. The RPD's questioning of the Appellant was frequently labored because of having to repeat or reframe questions in order to elicit an appropriate response. I note the Appellant appears to have only completed 5 years of schooling7, and that this might help to explain her manner of speaking during the hearing. I also note the XXXX report on file which states that the Appellant suffers from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.8 This also suggests that the Appellant was likely anxious during the hearing which could have affected her ability to formulate clear and coherent replies to the RPD's questions. Finally, I note that in her Counsel's final submissions to the RPD, her Counsel conceded that the Appellant was a "difficult historian" and suggested that this was likely due to "her own mental capacity".9

While I take all of these factors into account, I note that it would still be reasonable to expect that the Appellant's testimony provide a rough approximation of her narrative in terms of when events happened relative to one another, even if precision in the actual dates is not possible, and in terms of the order in which events occurred.

I therefore disagree with the RPD that the fact that the Appellant testified that her brother was after her even before 2008 signifies that there was a particularly serious omission from her BOC narrative. It seems more likely that she responded in the affirmative to what the RPD had asked without really thinking about it. Inconsistency regarding whether the Appellant lived in the house that she had built on her father's land

In the Appellant's BOC narrative, it is written: "En 2008, j'ai fait construire une petite maison sur un des terrains de mon pÞre ou j'habitais avec mes enfants. "10 However, at the hearing, the Appellant stated she never finished building the house and never lived in that house.11 Again, when confronted with the contradiction, the Appellant was only able to repeat that she had never lived in that house as it was not finished.12

The Appellant argues that there is no contradiction in this case, as the sentence in her BOC narrative can be interpreted in a way that does not contradict her testimony. The Appellant submits: "ln oral testimony, the appellant made it clear that she was living with her children on her father's land in her mother's house, as she had not completed construction of her house. The BOC narrative sentence, which was a translation to French and English through a Haitian Creole interpreter, bears both interpretations "ln 2008, I built a small house on one of my father's land where I lived with my children" is one possible interpretation. Another, equally valid interpretation of the sentence is "ln 2008, I built a small house on one of my father's land where I lived with my children." The appellant submits that when a sentence can be construed in one of two ways, one which is consistent with the appellant's sworn testimony, and another, which contradicts the appellant's sworn testimony, it is unreasonable, and contrary to the presumption of truth as set out in Maldonado for the Member to insist that there is only one possible interpretation which negates the appellant's credibility."13 (underlining in original)
I agree with the Appellant, I do not find that the contradiction to be sufficiently clear to warrant a finding that this diminishes the Appellant's credibility.

Though I find that the RPD erred in making this particular finding and in making the finding that the Appellant had omitted to include any reference to mistreatment from her brother prior to 2008, I do not find these errors to be determinative of the appeal. This is because the RPD was correct to note, during the hearing, several other problems with her testimony which alone are sufficient to find that her allegations are not credible.

At the hearing, the Appellant testified that after her brother attacked her and burned her house in December 2008, she left the family home in Gonaives to go to the town of Marchand where she rented a house. She stated she stayed there 6 months before her brother found her and began to persecute her by asking neighbours where she was living.14 The RPD then confronted the Appellant with the fact that according to her narrative she only felt obliged to leave the family home in 2012 after her mother had passed away and it was at that point that she moved to Marchand. Once confronted with this major contradiction, the Appellant simply stated that, she did live in Marchand in 2012. The RPD then asked her whether she had lived in Marchand before 2012, and the Appellant replied that she had not.15 The RPD reminded her that a few moments earlier she stated that she moved to Marchand in 2008, directly after she was attacked by her brother. The Appellant then replied that she had lived in a different house and moved from one house to another, both of which were in Marchand, in 2012.16 Finally, the RPD asked Counsel to show the Appellant her schedule A form on which she had marked the same address in Gonaives from XXXX 1996 to XXXX 2016.17

In my opinion, this confused and inconsistent testimony about what she did after ostensibly being attacked by her brother in 2008, is fatal to the Appellant's credibility. Despite the Appellant's limited education and anxiety level, it is reasonable to assume that she would know whether she left her family home directly after being attacked by her brother or some four years later, after her mother's death. It is also reasonable to assume that she would know where she resided in the intervening years between 2008 and when she departed Haiti for Brazil, at least in terms of how many years she spent at one address before moving on to another. Consequently, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's story of being persecuted by her brother is unworthy of belief. Weight given to the Appellant's interview after entering the United States

The Appellant was interviewed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) after entering the United States from Mexico, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. The interview was apparently conducted using the services of a Spanish interpreter. The notes of the interview are on the RPD file. The Appellant signed the interview notes on each page to attest to the truth of her statements. The notes reveal that the Appellant explained to the DHS officer that she was afraid to return to Haiti because there are no jobs and because she would like more money and a better future.18 The DHS notes make no mention of any problem or fears with regards to the Appellant's brother in Haiti.

The Appellant submits the RPD should not have given any weight to the DHS officer's interview notes. In the Appellant's memorandum, it states: "The appellant lived in Haiti for the vast majority of her life, and her native tongue is Haitian Creole. On her BOC she listed only Haitian Creole as a language she speaks. She spent some time in Brazil (where they speak Portuguese) and a brief time in Spanish speaking countries en route to the US. Even if the appellant can be assumed to have picked up some Spanish words en route to the United States, the US interview is clearly suspect and cannot reasonably be relied upon to impugn the appellant's credibility. See Wu v Canada (Citizenship and lmmigration),2010 FC 1102 (Canlll) at para 16 (...) the Board should be careful not to place undue reliance on the POE statements. The circumstances surrounding the taking of those statements is far from ideal and questions about their reliability will often arise."19

The RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation that she did not understand the DHS officer's questions which is why her replies were recorded incorrectly or were interpreted incorrectly. The RPD noted that much of the information recorded in the interview notes was accurate such as where she was living prior to entering the United States, information such as her children's names and dates of birth and information pertaining to other family members. The RPD reasoned that it is unlikely that the only questions which she failed to understand related to the reasons why she left Haiti. I agree with the RPD that, indeed, it seems unlikely that her lack of understanding of the questions was of such a selective nature. Nevertheless, unlike the RPD, I do not give the interview notes any weight nor do I take any adverse inference from these apparent contradictions, given that the language of interpretation was not one in which the Appellant is proficient.

Though I feel it was an error for the RPD to have given these notes weight, I do not find it to be determinative of the appeal, given my rationale for disbelieving the Appellant, outlined earlier in this decision. Weight given to the CASEC report

The Appellant submitted a letter from the "Conseil d'Administration de la Section Communale" (CASEC) for La Croix-Perisse. In the letter it states that on December 20, 2008, XXXX XXXX "a assassinÚ" the Appellant by stabbing her with a knife.20 The RPD asked the Appellant why the document states she was assassinated when, evidently, she is still alive. The Appellant replied that in Haiti, the term 'assasinÚ' means to be stabbed not assassinated. The RPD rejected this explanation as the letter from the CASEC was written in French, not in Creole, thus it would be reasonable to expect that the French meaning of the word was meant.

In her memorandum, the Appellant argues that: "Concerning the weight to be given to the CASEC report (para 27 of the decision), the appellant notes that it is consistent with the appellant's explanation of the local use of the word "assasins" that the CASEC report did not make any mention of finding a corpse when they attended at the scene."21

While it is true that the report does not make any mention of a corpse being discovered at the scene, it also does not mention that the Appellant was still alive when it went to investigate nor what happened to her after the attack. The report states that the council was informed of the incident by a XXXX XXXX XXXX and also notes that neighbours heard the perpetrator say: "He has to terminate her life."22
I agree with the RPD that given the apparent error and inconsistency in the report, the CASEC report should not be given any weight.

It should also be noted that the Appellant does not contest any of the RPD's other findings with regards to her supporting documentation. For instance, the RPD noted that her sister-in-law's letter states that the Appellant was attacked on December 20, 2011 instead of December 20, 2008, which was the date provided by the Appellant. 23 I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's supporting documents are either inconsistent with the Appellant's testimony or are insufficient in and of themselves to support the Appellant's allegations, given the serious issues with the credibility of her testimony. The RPD did not err with regards to the Appellant's documentation. Residual profile of the Appellant as a woman fearing gender-based persecution

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred when assessing her risks of gender-based persecution. The Appellant submits: "the Board looks at the appellant's residual profile as a woman in Haiti and concludes that her "resilience" will protect her from gender based persecution. With all due respect to the panel, there is no evidentiary basis upon which the panel can conclude that "resilient" women are less likely to be the victims of gender based persecution than less resilient women."24

I disagree with the Appellant. While the RPD does use the term 'resilience' it is not the only factor which is mentioned as contributing to the Appellant's risk of becoming a victim of gender-based persecution. The RPD also mentioned the presence of her family members, such as the Appellant's children, her sister-in-law who is looking after her children, her uncle as a male protector and the Appellant's history of adapting to new environments, as lived in Brazil, then Mexico, before entering the US in order to get to Canada.

Furthermore, as noted by the RPD, the Appellant did not argue a fear of gender-based persecution before the RPD, nor did she explain, in her memorandum to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), why she feels she would be at risk of gender-based persecution in returning to her country. Thus, even if the RPD erred in mentioning her 'resilience', the Appellant has not explained how this error would impact an allegation of risk.

I note that while gender-based violence is widespread in Haiti, the objective documentation indicates that the women who are most vulnerable to gender-based violence are those who were displaced since the 2010 earthquake, women from LGBT communities, young girls,25those living in poverty or slums, those who are unemployed, and those who do not have the protection of a male member of the family.26 The Appellant would not appear to fall into any of these categories. I also note that it is common in Haiti for women to be head-of-households, living alone or with children but without a male partner.27
I do not find that the RPD erred in its assessment of her residual profile.

After my independent review of the evidence in the Appellant's case, I find the RPD did not err in its finding that the Appellant's allegations are not credible. I am satisfied, based on the evidence, that the Appellant would not be personally subjected to a risk of torture, a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should she return to Haiti. I am also not satisfied the Appellant has demonstrated that there is a serious possibility that she would be persecuted on a Convention ground if she returned to Haiti at this time.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
